speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Members may also access the handout through the MP@SGPARL App.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Strong and stable families are the foundation upon which we nurture and build resilient individuals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A family is where we should feel safe and supported.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Unfortunately, some families are not a safe haven, as there is violence within the home.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: No one should experience violence, especially at the hands of a person whom they love and trust.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), globally, about one in three women worldwide have been subjected to either physical and/or sexual intimate partner violence or non-partner sexual violence in their lifetime.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: While these numbers are lower than global rates, we must aspire as a society to see that no one suffers from family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We saw in the past few years that the pandemic had cast a spotlight on family violence, given the added stress of balancing family responsibilities and work commitments amidst the heightened uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Of all the enquiries received by NAVH, an average of about 3,000 enquiries per year were related to abuse or violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Besides physical and sexual abuse, emotional and psychological abuse, such as exerting control over another's behaviour or victim blaming, is also a form of violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: While such abuse may be less visible or less understood, the harm that it causes to the survivor is no less significant.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Another reason why family violence is complex is because there is no single cause of family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Hence, the reasons for committing violence could be due to deep-seated issues, such as perpetrators themselves being abused or being a witness to violence in their own homes as a child or an inability to cope with stressors, such as unemployment, financial difficulties, parenting or other issues.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Medical or mental health conditions, addiction issues or disabilities may also impact one's ability to manage emotions in a healthy way.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The third cause as to why family violence is complex is because it often happens behind closed doors which makes it harder to detect.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Survivors may hesitate to seek help due to shame, stigma, fear of breaking up their family and the perception that family violence is a personal matter.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Similarly, individuals who observe family violence may remain as passive bystanders because they also consider it a private family matter.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Last but not least, family violence can have a detrimental impact on the next generation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Family violence goes against the fundamental values of our society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is why we are strengthening legislation to better protect survivors and enhance the rehabilitation and accountability of perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Once the protection and safety objectives have been achieved, we need to help perpetrators rehabilitate and families to heal relationships and reconcile.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This will help to break the cycle of violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In developing the strategies to tackle family violence, the Government consulted widely with experts and professionals from the healthcare, social services and legal sectors and members of the public to garner different perspectives and ideas to address this issue comprehensively.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We did this through the multi-stakeholder Taskforce on Family Violence which I co-chaired with Minister of State for Home Affairs, Assoc Prof Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim, from 2019 to 2021.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Taskforce's work culminated in its 16 recommendations released in September 2021.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Your views, ideas and feedback helped us to better understand the gaps in the family violence landscape and to co-create solutions to address them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Beyond the Taskforce, many from all walks of life, including survivors, perpetrators, friends and relatives of survivors of family violence, lawyers and healthcare workers, also shared their feedback, which helped us shape the amendments in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In particular, during the COVID-19 pandemic, you stepped up to keep families safe from violence, handling more than 4,500 enquiries and 1,100 cases in 2020 when we had the Circuit Breaker period, a notable increase from about 3,200 enquiries and 960 cases in 2019.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I would also like to thank our crisis shelters, Anglican Family Centre, Casa Raudha Women Home, Good Shepherd Centre and Star Shelter, for providing a safe haven for about 500 clients last year to recover from their trauma and regain confidence in living a life free from violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I also thank New Hope Community Services for providing temporary shelter to male survivors.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Additionally, I would like to acknowledge Lutheran Community Care Services for their efforts in providing a safe space for male survivors of family violence to discuss their experiences and widen their support networks.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I am deeply touched by the dedication of all our social service professionals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: You have invested much time and effort to support and keep survivors safe.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Some of you also work with perpetrators in their rehabilitation journey.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Sometimes, you yourself face risks because of the work that you do, especially when the family situation is volatile.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To increase awareness and strengthen societal attitudes against violence, MSF refreshed our Break the Silence public education campaign in 2021 to increase the awareness of different types of abuse, including non-physical abuse and to encourage survivors and bystanders to seek help.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As part of the refreshed campaign, we introduced the use of the "Signal for Help" hand sign that survivors can use to discreetly call for help.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To make it easier for survivors and the community to report violence and get immediate help, we now have an online channel as an additional mode of reporting to the 24-hour National Anti-Violence and Sexual Harassment Helpline.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Victim Care Cadre Programme has been offered to those below 18 years of age, to provide them with greater support during Police investigations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Home Team Community Assistance and Referral Scheme, otherwise known as HT CARES, which was piloted in Bedok Land Division in 2019, has been expanded to all Police Land Divisions since September 2021.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To strengthen protection and support for survivors, forensic-trained psychologists have been deployed to the Protection Specialist Centres since September 2022.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Selected Police officers from the Community Policing Unit have been appointed across the Police Land Divisions since July 2022, to specialise in the management of family violence cases and escalate potential high-risk cases for social intervention.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police also set up the Sexual Crime and Family Violence Command in April this year for better oversight of the management of sexual crime and family violence cases.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police Training Workgroup was set up by the Police and MSF in June 2021 to enhance training for frontline Police officers in engaging and managing family violence cases.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The training curriculum was co-developed with members of the Taskforce with professional experience and practice wisdom such as Family Service Centres, The Singapore Council of Women's Organisations, crisis shelters and the Family Justice Courts.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Women's Charter provides protection for all survivors of family violence, regardless of gender.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Since its enactment in 1961, the Women's Charter sets out how family and family relationships should be managed in statute.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Hence, the amendments are parked under the Women's Charter for historical reasons.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will need some time to consult the relevant stakeholders and will share more details when ready.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For now, the Bill with the proposed amendments will replace the family violence framework in the Women's Charter with a more comprehensive regime.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Under the Women's Charter, survivors may apply for a personal protection order, or PPO, to restrain their family members from committing further violence against them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Last year, about 2,000 PPO applications were made to the Family Justice Courts, of which 25% were made by men.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I will now elaborate on the key amendments made by the Bill, starting with the definition of family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The new section 58B updates the existing definition of "family violence" by making clear that family violence includes physical, sexual, emotional and psychological abuse.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The updated definition is aligned with how abuse is defined in other acts, such as the Children and Young Persons Act 1993 and the Vulnerable Adults Act 2018.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Bill makes clear that abuse may take the form of a single instance of conduct or behaviour, or a course of conduct or behaviour.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The definition of sexual abuse includes conduct or behaviour that coerces, or attempts to coerce, a person to engage in sexual activity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Illustrations on emotional or psychological abuse are given in the Bill, to raise understanding and aid discernment of these forms of abuse.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Stakeholders have shared situations where perpetrators threaten to withhold monthly allowance from their spouses, constantly call their spouses to check on their whereabouts and isolate them from their friends or family, including disallowing them to leave the house.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If the spouses do not comply, they may be threatened by the perpetrator.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These egregious forms of controlling behaviour – which falls within the definition of what some other jurisdictions call "coercive control" – can cause distress or mental harm to a survivor and would be considered emotional or psychological abuse under the new Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MSF had considered whether to include financial abuse in the definition of family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Financial abuse is a complex issue and subjected to different interpretations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We are working with relevant stakeholders and partners to study this issue further.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The updated definition of family violence would protect persons like Mrs B – a Long-Term Visit Pass Holder living in Singapore with her husband Mr B and their son.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr B would often exert power and control over his wife by threatening to chase her out of their house and not to renew her Long-Term Visit Pass, leaving her with no other physical or financial resource.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mrs B and her son had also suffered serious physical abuse from Mr B.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Due to the immense fear of Mr B's threats, Mrs B was afraid to apply for a PPO against her husband as it might result in her being chased out of the house and separated from her child.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The new amendments would provide greater assurance to people like Mrs B that such controlling behaviours is a form of abuse and that remedies are available for her.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Next, I will elaborate on the key provisions in clause 2, and these fall under three focal areas: (a) Focal Area One: empowering family violence survivors to better protect themselves; (b) Focal Area Two: strengthening the Government's ability to intervene in family violence cases; and (c) Focal Area Three: empowering the Court to make additional rehabilitative orders and strengthening enforcement against breaches including raising penalties.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The first focal area is on empowering family violence survivors to better protect themselves.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Unmarried persons aged 18 to below 21 years old will no longer need to rely on guardians, relatives, persons responsible for their care or persons appointed by the Minister to apply for a PPO on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The new section 63 also removes the need for them to act through a litigation representative.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These amendments ensure that survivors receive timely legal protection.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Today, the Court may issue a Counselling Order or a Domestic Exclusion Order together with a PPO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A Domestic Exclusion Order excludes a perpetrator from the entire or a part of the home.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, there have been cases where perpetrators continue to harass survivors outside their homes or make threats via text messages.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is in addition to Counselling and Domestic Exclusion Orders, which are already available.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The perpetrator who is subjected to a Stay Away Order cannot enter or remain in areas frequented by the survivor, such as a workplace, or a childcare centre where the survivor has enrolled their child.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A No Contact Order prohibits visits or communications with the survivor.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Court will make these orders if it is satisfied that it is necessary for the safety and protection of the survivor.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Breaches of these Court orders will be an arrestable offence punishable with an imprisonment and/or fine.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The new section 63B protects a survivor's identity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It prohibits any publication or broadcast – including on social media – that is likely to identify the survivor, unless the approval of the Director-General of Social Welfare and the consent of the survivor have been obtained.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Court will also be empowered to order the removal of any unauthorised publication or broadcast.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Failure to comply with a takedown order will be an offence punishable with a fine.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The second focal area is on strengthening the Government's ability to intervene in family violence cases.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MSF has statutory powers to protect children and vulnerable adults under the Children and Young Persons Act and Vulnerable Adults Act respectively.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In cases where an adult, such as a spouse or a parent who is not vulnerable under the Vulnerable Adults Act, is subjected to violence from another family member, the approach under the existing law is different.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The operative principle is to respect an adult survivor's right to self-determination.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The law only comes in when the adult survivor chooses to seek help from his or her relatives, friends or the community.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In recent times, social service agencies and the Government have encountered cases where adult survivors with mental capacity chose not to keep themselves safe, often putting themselves at risk of harm.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Bill empowers the Government to step in to protect such survivors and to intervene judiciously for their personal safety.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For this, the Bill grants powers to persons referred to as "protectors".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Protectors are persons with suitable qualifications and experience who are appointed by the Director-General of Social Welfare to carry out statutory duties and functions under the new Part 7.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In line with the Taskforce's recommendation, this will better protect the survivors at the onset of violence while further action is taken to ensure their safety, such as applying for a PPO or an Expedited Order or putting in place a safety plan.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: An Emergency Order will be issued if the protector is satisfied that there is a danger of the perpetrator committing family violence imminently against the survivor.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It takes effect immediately and is valid for 14 days to give the survivor time to apply for a PPO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Emergency Orders will be useful for persons such as Mr D, a 20-year-old tertiary student who was repeatedly hit and punched by his stepfather.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr D's mother was unable to protect him and the violence continued.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: With the help of social work professionals from the Protection Specialist Centre, he moved to a transitional shelter.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Though he was safe, he had to live apart from his mother and stepsiblings whom he wanted to continue living with.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In such cases, an Emergency Order would be issued to Mr D's stepfather immediately at the scene, restraining him from committing further violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A Domestic Exclusion Order could also be issued to prohibit Mr D's stepfather from being at home, thus, ensuring Mr D's safety while allowing him to continue living with his mother and stepsiblings.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Emergency Order is meant to be a stop gap measure.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: PPOs and other related Court Orders will continue to offer the main and longer-term protection against family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This period would give sufficient time for social service professionals to de-escalate the tension, put in place a safety plan for the survivor, provide the necessary intervention and allow the survivor to apply for a PPO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The new sections 59 to 59E introduce provisions for MSF to obtain information about family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Protectors will be allowed to assess and obtain information on whether a person has experienced or is at risk of experiencing family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They will be conferred powers to enter the home to make an assessment where needed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A protector will also be empowered to direct an individual to disclose information or provide relevant records relating to the person who has experienced or is experiencing family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Those who report suspected family violence cases to protectors, the Police or other authorised persons will be protected from criminal or civil liability if they have acted in good faith and with reasonable care.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is to encourage more people to step forward to report family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The next group of amendments aim to protect survivors who are at risk of danger but are unwilling to take action to protect themselves.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members may recall a 2017 case of a 30-year-old master's degree student who physically abused his 68-year-old mother, Mdm Y.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He starved her, did not allow her to shower or to make noise when he was stressed with his studies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He also hit her face and assaulted her private parts with a metal padlock and with his knee.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Despite being hospitalised multiple times for serious injuries and being placed in a safe house, Mdm Y insisted on returning home.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As she did not want to implicate her son, she did not attribute the injuries to his conduct.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: She also did not retaliate whenever he took out his frustrations on her.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This Bill will better protect persons like Mdm Y.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Currently, a family member, guardian or relative or appointed persons can only step in to apply for PPOs on behalf of survivors below 21 years of age or who are incapacitated.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, as seen in Mdm Y's case, not all survivors will choose to keep themselves safe, sometimes due to the perpetrator exerting undue influence over the survivor.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Allowing protectors to apply for PPOs and other orders on behalf of a survivor will strengthen the protection for survivors whose safety is seriously threatened but who refuse to apply for a PPO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The new section 60C allows protectors to apply to the Court for electronic monitoring.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Electronic monitoring, which could include e-tagging, will be used against high-risk perpetrators in exceptional cases, where there is reasonable suspicion that a PPO has been breached with harm inflicted on the survivor, and the survivor has not taken steps to protect himself or herself.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It has been used by the Police for accused persons released on Court bail.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Through e-tagging, the authorities can be alerted if, for example, a perpetrator with Domestic Exclusion Order made against him or her enters the survivor's home, so action can be taken quickly.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As electronic monitoring is intended for high-risk perpetrators, only protectors may apply for electronic monitoring, after an assessment is made on the circumstances of each case.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Details of the electronic monitoring regime will be worked on further by MSF.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As a last resort and when all other interventions fail, the new section 60D allows protectors to apply to the Court to remove a survivor from his or her home.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Court must be satisfied that a Removal Order is necessary for the protection or personal safety of the survivor.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: When making a Removal Order, the Court must also make a Care Order, a Supervision Order, or both of these Orders.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A Care Order commits the survivor to the care of a fit person.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A Supervision Order places the survivor under the supervision of a protector or another suitable person appointed by the Court for a specified period.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Court may also make an order against the survivor, prohibiting the survivor from returning home, or visiting or communicating with the perpetrator.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Prohibiting the survivor from returning home is to protect the survivor from potential further harm.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If the survivor is removed from his or her home, the survivor may be admitted into a residential facility, such as a crisis shelter.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It will not be an offence if the survivor contravenes these orders, but the contravention must be taken into account by the Court when deciding whether to vary, suspend or revoke a Care Order or Supervision Order.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will also ensure that adequate intervention is provided to the survivor prior to, during and after his or her removal, to mitigate any negative impact the removal might have on the survivor.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In the earlier case of Mdm Y who was severely abused by her 30-year-old son and who did not take steps to protect herself, with the new amendments, a protector would be able to apply for a PPO with a Domestic Exclusion Order against her son to prohibit him from returning home, even if Mdm Y does not consent.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The protector may make a Police report if there is a breach of the PPO or the Domestic Exclusion Order.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A breach of these orders is an arrestable offence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In addition, if there is reasonable suspicion that the PPO or Domestic Exclusion Order has been breached with harm inflicted on the survivor, the protector may also apply for Electronic Monitoring for her son.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As a last resort, if all interventions fail, a protector can apply to the Court for Mdm Y to be removed from her home.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If granted, she will be placed in a crisis shelter for a specified period until it is safe for her to return home.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It was not easy for MSF and the Taskforce to formulate this group of amendments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Government would rather not have to introduce such powers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, real-life cases show that complex dynamics exist between perpetrators and survivors.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Giving due weight to the principle of protecting lives and preventing further harm, the Government, therefore, carefully calibrated the amendments under Focal Area Two.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Necessary safeguards are put in place to strike a balance between pushing the legal frontiers of protection for survivors and avoiding statutory over-reach.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The third Focal Area is on empowering the Court to make additional rehabilitative orders, raise penalties and strengthen enforcement against breaches of family violence-related offences.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Not only do survivors need a supportive environment to heal from their trauma, perpetrators also need a safe environment where they can share their struggles openly, without being judged.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This set of amendments aims to address the root causes of family violence perpetration and to provide the necessary support to perpetrators in their rehabilitation journey.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: With appropriate support and intervention, perpetrators can learn to better manage their emotions and behaviours and to break the cycle of violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: During last year's National Family Violence Networking System Conference, I met a group of men from Thye Hua Kwan Family Service Centre's Brotherhood Programme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This programme supports males who had past histories of aggressive episodes towards their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These men were supported to examine the consequences of their aggression on their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: With the support of fellow male participants, they experienced positive behavioural changes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: During the Conference, the participants of this programme sung a self-composed song titled, "A Better Man".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A tiny seed of hope is crying to see.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: With a heart of gold and all the love in the world, give us one more chance to start again." I applaud these individuals who took the bold step to try to become a better person for themselves, their families, friends and the community.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MSF and our community partners are committed to supporting perpetrators, whether male or female, in their rehabilitation journey.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Currently, to rehabilitate perpetrators, the Court may make a Counselling Order when it issues a PPO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A person under a Counselling Order, and this may be the perpetrator, survivor, or a child is required to attend a counselling programme offered by social service agencies appointed by MSF.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: With a greater focus on rehabilitation of perpetrators, the new section 60E expands the scope of the existing Counselling Order to include other programmes, treatments and interventions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These include parenting programmes, caregiver training, or family therapy and other programmes which cater better to the risk levels and unique needs of each perpetrator.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Counselling will help perpetrators such as Mr Y, caregiver of his wheelchair-bound mother.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Y threatened his mother with a knife and threw away her medication as he did not think the medication was effective.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Through the Court-ordered mandatory counselling, Mr Y gained insight into his mother's care needs and the impact of his actions on her.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He also completed a caregiver training to better care for his mother.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Upon the completion of the mandatory counselling sessions, Mr Y voluntarily continued with additional counselling sessions and showed significant improvement in his behaviour.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Y and his mother now enjoy a better relationship with no further incidence of violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, counselling may not be effective for all persons.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The MSF study on the Intergenerational Transmission of Criminality and Other Social Disadvantages, which I referred to earlier, found that among those who had PPO applications made against them, approximately 14% had been diagnosed with mental health conditions prior to the first PPO application.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Bill lists several conditions which must be fulfilled, before the Court can make a Mandatory Treatment Order.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This takes reference from the Mandatory Treatment Order regime under the Protection from Harassment Act.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, the Court may call for a specified psychiatrist to provide a preliminary assessment report for the Court to decide if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the perpetrator is likely to be suffering from a psychiatric condition and that the psychiatric condition is likely to be a contributing factor for that person committing family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If the Court considers that reasonable grounds exist, the Court must call for a formal assessment report on the perpetrator by an appointed psychiatrist.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The psychiatrist must assess and report on: firstly, whether the perpetrator is suffering from a psychiatric condition; secondly, that the condition is a contributing factor for the perpetrator's commission of family violence which was the basis of his or her PPO; thirdly, that the psychiatric condition must be susceptible to treatment; and lastly, whether the perpetrator is suitable for treatment.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Bill also specifies other factors the psychiatrist must consider.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A Mandatory Treatment Order can only be made if the psychiatrist's formal assessment report certifies that all these factors are met.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Currently, when a PPO has been revoked or has expired, the Counselling Order will also cease to have effect and this will no longer be the case after we pass the amendments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Under the Bill, a Counselling Order and a Mandatory Treatment Order will survive the PPO, so that the necessary interventions can be completed to ensure that the root cause of family violence is addressed, to avoid recurrence of family violence against current or future family members.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Bill also introduces factors that the Court must consider before revoking a PPO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Where a Counselling Order or a Mandatory Treatment Order was made, the Court must consider any report by the counselling agency or the appointed psychiatrist.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Court will also consider if there remains a risk of family violence and whether the survivor's consent to the revocation was made voluntarily.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To ensure perpetrators take their rehabilitation seriously, we will strengthen enforcement and penalties against breaches of Court orders.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, the Bill increases the penalties for breaches of family violence-related Court orders.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For a first conviction, the offender can be fined or imprisoned, or both.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On conviction, an offender can be fined or imprisoned, or both.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The penalties will minimally be on par with the enhanced penalties for breaches of Protection orders under the Protection from Harassment Act where the victim is a vulnerable person or is or was in an intimate relationship with the offender.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This amendment arose in response to stakeholders' feedback that some perpetrators did not take Counselling Orders seriously, including not turning up for counselling sessions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Currently, the survivor may apply for an order of committal against the perpetrator, if the perpetrator does not attend counselling.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, as there are several court procedures involved, survivors may be deterred from doing so.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To hold perpetrators accountable, breaches of Counselling Orders and Mandatory Treatment Orders will be an offence, with the perpetrator liable to a fine on conviction.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The new sections 64 to 64G introduce new powers to enable MSF's enforcement officers to detect and investigate offences under the new Part 7.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These powers include powers to enter premises or seize documents for evidence of an offence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: (In Mandarin):   As a society, we cannot tolerate family violence occurring in our communities, nor can we turn a blind eye to family violence just because it happens within individual families or in hidden corners.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The definition of family violence has been updated to make clear that it encompasses physical, sexual, psychological and emotional abuse.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Next, I will raise a few real-life cases to highlight how the new Bill protects survivors of family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, a Long-Term Visit Pass holder was constantly threatened by her husband to chase her out of the house and not to renew her Long-Term Visit Pass, leaving her with no financial resource.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Due to the immense fear of being chased out of the house and being separated from her child, she was afraid to apply for a PPO against her husband.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The new amendment will provide greater assurance to such vulnerable groups, as such controlling behaviours constitute a form of abuse under the updated definition of family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is because in cases of family violence we have observed, the perpetrator may not only inflict harm within the home, but also go to the survivor's frequented places, such as their workplace, a childcare centre where their child is enrolled, or harass the survivor through electronic devices.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The newly introduced Stay Away Order and No Contact Order will prohibit such behaviours.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In addition, adult survivors with mental capacity may also choose not to keep themselves safe and put themselves at risk of harm.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To tackle such scenarios, the Bill empowers the Government to intervene judiciously to protect these survivors' personal safety.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Real-life cases show that complex dynamics do exist between perpetrators and survivors, and there will be some survivors who choose not to protect themselves from harm.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, in a family violence incident that occurred in 2017, a 30-year-old Master's degree student physically abused his 68-year-old mother.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He starved her, did not allow her to shower, and even hit her face and assaulted her private parts with a metal padlock.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Despite being hospitalised multiple times for serious injuries and being placed in a safe house, the mother insisted on returning home.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As she did not want to implicate her son, she did not report these incidents to the Police.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: She also did not retaliate whenever he committed violence or took out his frustrations on her.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is to strengthen the protection for survivors whose safety is seriously threatened, but refuse to apply for a PPO.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In addition to enhancing protection for survivors, we will also enhance the rehabilitation of perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Our ultimate goal is to help families affected by family violence heal from their trauma.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These include parenting programmes, caregiver training, family therapy or other programmes which cater better to the risk levels and unique needs of perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, in one case, the son was the caregiver of his wheelchair-bound mother.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He threatened his mother with a knife and threw away her medication as he did not think the medication was effective.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Through the Court-ordered mandatory counselling, the son gained insight into his mother's care needs and the impact of his actions on her.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He completed a caregiver training to better care for his mother.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Today, their relationship has improved with no further incidents of violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It also supports families affected by family violence towards reconciliation and healing, to enable them to return to their normal lives.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, the other amendments made by the Bill are sufficiently described by the explanatory statement and I will not go into them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This Bill reflects the Government's strong stance against violence and our commitment to keeping families safe, in partnership with the community and the general public.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We aim to address the risks and needs of both survivors and perpetrators and support them towards family reconciliation where possible.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Bill builds on past efforts by the Government and the social service sector to tackle family violence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is a whole-of-society effort where everyone has a part to play to help families break the cycle of violence.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One of the areas which I support is the protection of the survivor's identity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a general rule, for all matters relating to personal information, consent is key.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If a person consents to have their stories published, then it should be allowed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This general rule is especially salient for persons who have experienced trauma.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There need not, however, be a symmetry about this.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The privacy of the perpetrator does not qualify for the same level of protection automatically.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For one, there should be some deterrent effect if such offenders knew that their names would be made public.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The need to be protected from re-offenders must be weighted in our consideration.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A second point I want to deal with has to do with the power of the Director General of Social Welfare.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yet, we often think of the family in abstract terms and, quite often, for the positive force it exerts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yet, violence, domination, pain, harm and abuse also occur within the walls of a family.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to be vigilant and sensitive in our approach.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Hard rules and automatic application of these rules are a poor response to the challenges that we face today.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our framework has evolved to a more nuanced and sophisticated one that requires more use of discretion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill also gives the Court powers to issue a broader range of orders in domestic violence situations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The value of this cannot be overstated if we recall a past incident in 2004 when an offender confronted his spouse at her workplace at Tuas and killed her there.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another new form of Court order is the "No Contact Order" that will protect the victim from being harassed by the offender, not just physically but through other means of communication.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another aspect of the Bill is more effective monitoring of orders issued, for example, possibly requiring those subject to orders to wear electronic monitoring devices.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe that such certainty of detection will deter breaches of Court orders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides the contents of the provisions, MSF has also reviewed feedback from the public and consulted many stakeholders, including Family Service Centres, crisis shelters, healthcare workers and lawyers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I have two concerns that I wish to raise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the Bill makes it clear that MSF is the lead Ministry on domestic violence, with the Police and MHA playing a somewhat secondary role.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, my understanding of the 24-hour DVERT is that it will be staffed by MSF, with the Police coming along to attend cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, any emergency orders issued by DVERT will not be issued by the Police, but by MSF officers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This apparent secondary role for the Police leads me to worry that calls for Police assistance in domestic situations, however serious, may be passed on to MSF automatically or risk being no-crimed in the Police records.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Suppose a report is received that a person has threatened to harm his or her spouse with a knife and, upon agencies arriving at the scene, the presence of the knife is confirmed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This scenario should properly be classified as criminal intimidation, which is an arrestable offence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Someone calls for assistance due to domestic violence and, upon arrival, the response team sees that the injury is serious and may be a case of voluntarily causing grievous hurt, another arrestable offence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In these scenarios, would the Police handle the matter as it would normally do if the parties were unrelated to each other, that is, classify the cases accordingly as criminal intimidation and voluntarily causing grievous hurt, arrest the suspect and possibly charge the person in Court with the appropriate offence under the Penal Code?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Or would DVERT see it as basically a case of family violence to be proceeded with under the Women's Charter, thereby inadvertently downgrading the seriousness of the incidents?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second clarification I have is on the tremendous demand on manpower that the provisions will entail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The explanatory statement to the Bill has confirmed that the Bill will involve the Government in extra financial expenditure, the exact amount of which cannot at present be ascertained.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Has MSF projected how many more staff will be needed to implement the provisions of this Bill?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some of the provisions will entail round-the-clock teams, such as DVERT.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They also need to be highly trained, as attending to such cases will involve tense situations and may expose officers to physical danger.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for the Police, they are expected to support DVERT's work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are all aware of the longstanding manpower challenges at frontline policing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government intend to meet the significant manpower demands that the Bill entails?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will strengthen our ability to intervene in family violence and allow for stronger enforcement against breaches of protective measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen the consequences on lives when our measures fall short of protecting families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope these amendments will allow us to act quickly and more proactively to keep families safe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first set of clarifications are on the manpower needed for implementation and enforcement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The increased protection and enforcement powers under the Bill will require trained manpower.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The protector must be sensitive to the needs of family violence survivors, be able to make decisions with limited information and make quick decisions that balance the interests of all parties involved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State clarify the qualifications and experience required of a protector?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share what training will be introduced for protectors?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond creating the position of the protector, can the Minister of State share whether there is sufficient current manpower to implement the expanded powers under the Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not, what is the shortfall and what are MSF's plans to make up for this shortfall?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the individuals covered under the protection order.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 60A allows the Court to make a protection order if an aggressor has committed or is likely to commit family violence against an individual.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When such a protected individual is the guardian or parent of minor children or otherwise vulnerable family members, it seems likely that those dependants are likely to be in the same household and face the same threats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be burdensome to require fresh applications for the individual's dependants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State clarify whether when a protection order is granted to protect a caregiver of vulnerable family members, should the Court also automatically consider issuing protection orders to protect those vulnerable family members?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third clarification is on the use of electronic monitoring.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given the potential intrusiveness of electronic monitoring, can the Minister of State clarify when electronic monitoring will be deemed necessary?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Bilateral monitoring where both the perpetrator and the survivor are tracked has been used in countries, such as the United Kingdom and Australia.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: NGOs have raised to me that this may jeopardise victims' privacy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If victims do not understand how the monitoring is carried out, it may cause unnecessary anxiety about their locations being revealed to perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share about the types of electronic monitoring arrangements that will be introduced?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are there any plans to introduce bilateral electronic monitoring?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share how electronic monitoring will be used to detect breaches of other types of orders under the Bill or other family violence offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State also share which agencies or individuals will have access to the data from electronic monitoring?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And what safeguards will be in place to prevent the abuse the use of such data?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My fourth clarification is on the use of policing to complement protection and other family violence orders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Paper orders may not be sufficient to deter some offenders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Increased monitoring and risk of detection may serve as more practical deterrence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share if there are any plans to arrange appropriate levels of policing by the Police to complement protection and other types of family violence orders?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, is there a protocol for increased policing by the Police to be automatically arranged where protection or other types of orders are in place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My fifth and final clarification is on the arrangements to ensure continued protection after an aggressor has served jail term for offences of family violence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The punishment for a family violence may include imprisonment of 12 months or for aggravated offences,18 months.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The imprisonment term serves as punishment for the aggressor.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But for survivors of family violence, the imprisonment only protects them for as long as the aggressor is in prison.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the aggressor is in prison, there will be no instances that show the likelihood of the aggressor committing family violence since they are in jail.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There may not be any factual basis for the survivor then to apply to Court for a Protection Order or other family violence orders, since there is no recent evidence of the aggressor being likely to commit family violence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share how any imprisonment for offences of family violence will affect Protection Orders and other types of family violence orders?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What arrangements will be made while this offender is in prison and after the offender's release for the survivor's continued protection?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure this is something which all of us do on a weekly basis during our Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In preparing for this speech, I am reminded of a number of victims of family violence and abuse who have sought our assistance and some of the imagery of bruises and injuries sustained from physical violence, the ridiculous verbal and psychological abuses that they have suffered and the trauma and fear that is in our residents' eyes and voice, even as they muster up enough courage to relate some of their experiences to me.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am thankful to the various agencies including MSF who have done what they can to provide timely assistance to our residents who have sought our help.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, in this regard, I am supportive of this Bill to introduce a more comprehensive regime to protect against family violence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To start with, of course, family violence and abuse can take many forms beyond physical hurt and harassment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would be a more comprehensive and practical definition rather than the narrow and prescriptive definition previously.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My speech today will be focused on the need for greater assurance and more timely support for families at risk or are in domestic violence situations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise the merits of protecting victims through better protections, while enhancing rehabilitation of perpetrators of family violence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Having a second layer of protection through electronically monitoring arrangements also enable enforcement officers to be in a better position to ensure survivors feel and receive a level of personal safety and security.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the plans to strengthen rehabilitation of perpetrators through counselling and treatment orders are also commendable in allowing families to find and resolve the root cause of domestic violence and abuse.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the amendments and new provisions introduced by the Bill, I have a number of queries I wish to clarify with the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Family violence will have far-reaching and traumatic consequences in every aspect of a person's life at any age, whether they are above or below the age of 18.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Trauma often force children to mature faster and beyond their years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A 17-year-old going through a similar abusive situation as an 18-year-old will have the same need and want to have that autonomy to decide to protect themselves from domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, children from the age of 13 can even take up employment in a non-industrialised setting and some may have had to juggle schoolwork with part-time employment just to supplement the family income.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In cases where someone is under the age of 18, is not married and does not have any other older family member who can file a PPO application on their behalf, to whom can they turn to for assistance?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More broadly, how can we ensure that children do not fall through the cracks?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, in cases involving a domestic exclusion order, a stay away order or a no contact order under the new section 60B, how can we ensure that there is no financial strain or damage caused to survivors?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While we are moving towards a cashless society, there could be cases where women and children do not have access to the family's finances or do not have friends and extended family they can feel comfortable turning to, with the perpetrator either being unwilling to provide for financial support or simply unable to given that he may be remanded.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, while I recognise the need to "break the cycle of violence" through rehabilitative and treatment provisions, could there be more room to consider the needs and wants of survivors, rather than via the Courts instead?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is not to say we do not give offenders a second chance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While there could be many cases where there is a strong desire on both the perpetrators and survivors to heal the relationship, some may not wish to confront the intimidating and traumatic prospects of repairing this broken relationship.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At present, the Court may already require the survivor, perpetrator of family violence and/or their children to attend mandatory counselling.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am appreciative of the enhanced powers to take timely interventions to safeguard the health and well-being of victims of family abuse.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I believe that there needs to be a longer-term game plan to prevent family violence in the first place and provide greater lasting support to victims, especially those with psychological trauma and physical displacement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For every case that is surfaced, there could be many more that are suffering in silence and more who do not know who they can trust or turn to for assistance, particularly when the ones they loved the most turned out to be the ones causing them such intolerable harm.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For victims of family violence, we need to provide for more structural forms of assistance, longer-term assistance especially, as it relates to psychological trauma or physical displacement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Often, family violence survivors choose to endure the abuse, instead of reporting their abusers to the Police in fear of either further abuse or being left homeless and vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, if one considers Maslow's hierarchy of needs, it is only after physiological needs of food, water, shelter, clothing and a place to sleep are met can one begin to consider safety and security in their family.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Survivors of family violence face a very real dilemma when reporting their abusers, as this could also mean a loss of basic needs, especially if the abuser is the sole breadwinner of the family.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to ensure that survivors will not feel worse off when they finally break their silence and that adequate support are available and ready for them when they do find themselves in a situation needing them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Mental health and psychological support in the form of counselling or therapeutic support is also essential during this trying period.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Particularly for women and children who are not locals and are on long-term visit passes, for example, their right to feel safe and have a safe place to live in is a precarious one without the support of their local spouse, not knowing when they might have to leave this place they call home.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And yet, even as they can continue to reside here, their ability to access affordable housing through the Housing and Development Board (HDB) ownership or rentals is also not a given.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must therefore recognise that holistic support is vital to enable survivors to complete their journey towards full recovery from family violence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Road rage cases are increasingly common, the latest high-profile case being that involving a car driving off with a cyclist who laid on the bonnet after a heated argument between the two women involved.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Last month, two elderly men were arrested after a fight broke out over cigarette butts in a coffeeshop.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And online, we have trolls masquerading behind a pseudonym, spreading hatred, anger, personal attacks and verbal abuse, often in a coordinated and organised manner.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It may be idealistic for me to say we need to heal the world and make it a better place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But as leaders of this country, I think there is much food for thought here and it is upon us to demonstrate what Singapore society should be.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my years volunteering in the community legal clinics and during weekly Meet-the-People Session prior to becoming a Member of Parliament, I have come across several such cases where spouses live in constant fear of their other half, while continuing to stay together with no way out of their predicament.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I remember vividly a case which I attended to almost a decade ago when I was a newly called junior lawyer, where a foreign spouse visited the community legal clinic, crying.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She shared with me that she had been subjected to her husband's verbal and physical abuse for years.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At first, she decided to tolerate the mistreating for the sake of their young children and due to her worry of her husband cancelling the sponsorship for her permanent residency (PR) status to remain in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, her husband's treatment towards her continued to worsen, to the extent that he forbade her to step out of the house and would lock her and her children indoors whenever he headed out to work his night shifts.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On that particular night when she came to see me, she managed to sneak out of the house and came to my legal clinic to seek advice on divorce, as her mother-in-law, who had a spare key, had come to the flat to visit the grandchildren.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent years, there have been increased efforts on the ground to raise awareness on the personal protection order (PPO).

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: More community legal clinics have been set up at places, such as Community Centres across the heartlands and neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since the COVID-19 period, Pro Bono SG has also begun to offer virtual legal consultations for the convenience of residents who may, due to family circumstances, be unable to attend the legal clinic session in person.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In our Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC, in conjunction with the Law Awareness Weeks@CDC last year, our M3 volunteers organised a physical law awareness talk at Woodgrove's Fuchun CC, where we invited lawyers and senior social workers from PAVE to share in both Malay and English languages, about what constitutes family violence, what are the types of assistance and support available to counter domestic violence.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At MSF's front, just as what Minister of State Sun shared earlier, we have also seen the establishment of the National Anti-Violence and Sexual Harassment Helpline (NAVH) and online channels, as well as the setting up of more Family Service Centres and Protection Specialist Centres that encourage victims of family violence to not suffer in silence and to take action in putting things to an end.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have also seen more collaborations between the Ministry and the community to raise more awareness in this aspect.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One example is our Woodgrove Division's collaboration with the Family Justice Courts last August on the Family Justice @ Heartlands series where several expert panelists, including the Registrar of the Family Justice Courts, a representative from the Rehabilitation and Protection Group from MSF and esteemed lawyers, were invited to come together to share their insights on the holistic support available on protection related matters.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am heartened by this ongoing collaborative effort to reach out to our community at large and applaud those additional measures which will be introduced through this amendment Bill.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I would also like to take this opportunity to seek some clarifications.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Take, for example, a 16-year-old teenage girl who has been exposed to domestic violence alongside her mother.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In an attempt to keep the family intact, the mother refuses to apply for a PPO for herself and her daughter against the father.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For cases such as this, to whom can this 16-year-old seek help from if she has no other family members to rely on?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can a protector be activated in such an instance?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My second point, the workability of certain court orders imposed against the accused perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In typical situations, however, where a husband and wife with limited income are staying under the same roof, imposing such orders may seem either impractical or inconvenient to one party.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, it forces the perpetrator to move out of the matrimonial home, with no alternate accommodations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While I know that MSF provides shelters for victims of family violence, would assistance be also rendered to perpetrators in cases where the Court has imposed such restraining orders as well?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My third point, the prevention of the abuse of the system.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not too far-fetched to assume that parties with acrimonious marriages may take the opportunity to cause difficulties or disrupt plans if given the ability to do so.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In order to ensure that the system remains fair and partial, we will need to ensure that it cannot be manipulated in such a way that spouses can use it as a form of revenge.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us all continue to work together towards preserving the spirit of therapeutic justice, to habilitate and restore broken relationships amongst family members, in the best interests and welfare of our children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In particular, I commend the work of MSF and the Taskforce on Family Violence led by Minister of State Sun Xueling and Minister of State Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim for the comprehensive recommendations in the task force's report of 2021.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MSF has been in extensive consultations with various stakeholders, including crisis shelter homes like Casa Raudha, which provides interim protection for vulnerable women and children facing family violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over the years, we have seen various legislative enhancements and steps to raise awareness on this important issue, one which lies close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is something that I had raised before in this House.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, a survivor must apply in Court for a PPO and at the time of application, be granted an expedited order.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Unfortunately, this presents a time gap between the initial incident of family violence and the issuance of the expedited order or a PPO.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is an important development because every survivor faces unique circumstances that may impact their willingness or ability to pursue legal remedies such as a PPO.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some survivors may feel that applying for a PPO may escalate the violence or place them in greater danger while others may not want to involve the legal system for fear of causing the perpetrator to be jailed, thus further complicating the issues with the perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope a nuanced approach can be taken in exercising this power by the protector to apply for a PPO, especially in cases where survivors are reluctant to do so on their own accord.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Legal remedies such as PPOs should be a measure of last resort and only issued when it is assessed that there is high risk that the survivor's safety being compromised.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, it must be remembered that beyond legal redress and intervention, the Ministry and its affiliates, partners and agencies already provide holistic support and resources to meet survivors' needs such as counseling, advocacy and safety planning.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the enhanced support in this regard through this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By providing a range of support services that address the unique needs and circumstances of survivors, we can help empower survivors to take control of their lives and make informed decisions about their safety and well-being.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another change is that the Bill creates a new protection order that can include a number of provisions such as an order to stay away from the survivor and to have no contact with the survivor.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Allow me to share a story about a family violence survivor in Casa Raudha called Mdm N.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She is a foreign bride who suffered spousal abuse and sought refuge with her five-year old son at the shelter through MSF's help.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Typically, she will bring her son to work.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, one day, the child's paternal grandfather and paternal aunt came to Mdm N's workplace and took the child without her consent.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Even after the matter was reported and the Police interviewed her son and her husband's family, the family refused to cooperate to return the son back to Mdm N.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At that time, it was assessed that Mdm N's son was not in any immediate danger while in the company of her estranged husband's family and her husband, and that her husband has every right to have care and control of the son at that time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This separation from her five-year-old son caused a lot of anguish for Mdm N and inflicted on her more pain and hurt than any previous injuries that she had suffered at the hands of the perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the amendments in this Bill, had a Stay Away or No Contact order been made, such incidents and interventions by other third parties like extended relatives or family members would have been prevented.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would further strengthen the support for family violence survivors and their children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I thus feel that the amendments in this Bill are timely.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The changes may not have come in time for Mdm N, but it would be helpful for other mothers who stand in similar shoes in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I thus welcome the changes to this Bill to better protect all survivors of family violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Under the current Women's Charter section 64, subsections (a) and (b), the definition of "family violence" refers to placing a family member in fear of hurt or causing hurt to the family member. "Hurt" in turn means bodily pain, disease or infirmity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is also an element of intention on the part of the offender, in that the offender must wilfully or knowingly place the family member in fear of hurt or must have caused hurt by an act which is known to result in hurt.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The element of intention also appears to have been removed as there will be family violence so long as the conduct causes injury or pain.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, I note that this definition of family violence is principally adapted from the definition of abuse in the Vulnerable Adults Act (VAA).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The VAA is meant to protect vulnerable adults, that is, individuals incapable of protecting themselves, whereas family violence provisions may apply to all adults, including those who are capable of protecting themselves.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Further, would there be any guidance on how the new broadened family violence definition should be interpreted?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There should be clarity to this, given that upon belief that there is family violence or risk of family violence, the protector has wide-ranging powers, including the powers to: (a) assess a victim; (b) enter premises; (c) apply to Court for PPO; and, in high-risk situations, (d) make emergency orders against persons they believe to have committed family violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I turn to the powers of the Domestic Violence Emergency Response Team and the protector.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are there any safeguards against the abuse of such powers?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Where a child is involved, it potentially involves removing a parent accused of being a perpetrator from the child's life.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These are drastic orders that are capable of disrupting and impacting children's lives.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, if all measures are insufficient to protect the family violence survivor, the protector can also apply to Court to remove the survivors for their safety.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is a concern that this would deter survivors from seeking help if they are not ready to move out.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I humbly suggest that there should be greater public awareness and counselling of families involved to assure them that these measures are of a last resort.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is consistent with the case law in relation to a care and protection order under the Children and Young Persons Act, where such measures are of last resort.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also note that there would be the use of e-tagging in deterring family violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is something that I had raised in a Parliamentary Question to the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) on 1 March last year for the use of tagging technology to alert survivors in close range to high risk or violent ex-offending perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that e-tagging and the use of other technology may act as a deterrence to perpetrators and assurance to survivors of their safety and protection.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, besides punitive measures and deterrence, we must not forget the potential for the rehabilitation of perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Together with Casa Raudha, Keat Hong Community Centre organises annual talks for men to tackle issues of patriarchal mindsets, toxic masculinity and equal parenting responsibilities in our efforts to end family violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In one session, I had the opportunity to speak to a panelist who was a former perpetrator himself.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He shared how he was truly repentant and wanted to reconcile with his wife and family.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He committed himself to a path of atonement and forgiveness from his family.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Now, with every passing day, he tries to become a better husband, a better father, a better man.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that besides working to protect survivors of family violence, we can also continue to consider greater rehabilitation and reconciliation efforts in the future to bring former perpetrators on the path of recovery and rehabilitation, so that one day they can be welcomed back in the lives of those whom they had loved, lost and hurt before.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked how the updated definition of family violence should be interpreted.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Family violence comprises the broad categories of abuse that our social service professionals typically encounter – specifically, physical, sexual and emotional or psychological abuse.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Bill makes clear the type of conduct or behaviour that amounts to each type of abuse.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, a survivor should be able to obtain a personal protection order (PPO) against a perpetrator who turns violent under the influence of drugs or alcohol, even though he might not fully know the effect of his actions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
